analysis.one_liner: Raises the corporate tax rate for companies whose CEO pay exceeds 50 times their typical worker's pay.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would add up to 5 percentage points to the 21% corporate tax rate at firms with extreme CEO-to-worker pay gaps, was introduced with 30 Democratic members and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which has not acted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies with more than 50 employees would pay a higher federal corporate tax rate — on top of the current 21% — if their chief executive's pay is more than 50 times what their median worker makes. The surcharge grows with the gap: half a point above 50-to-1, up to 5 points above 500-to-1. Large private companies with $100 million or more in annual revenue would have to report their pay ratio too, and the bill directs Treasury to write rules to stop companies from dodging the tax by swapping employees for contractors. It applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large corporations, especially low- and mid-wage employees at firms where the CEO earns hundreds of times their pay. The tax creates a financial incentive for companies to narrow the gap, either by raising typical workers' pay or reining in executive pay. It also raises federal revenue that funds public services.

how_it_helps.text: Companies with a pay ratio above 50-to-1 face a corporate tax surcharge of 0.5 to 5 percentage points on top of the 21% rate, scaling with the size of the gap — so a company at 600-to-1 pays 26% instead of 21%.

The pay ratio is measured over a rolling five-year average using the SEC's existing executive compensation disclosure rules, and it applies to the highest-paid employee even if that person is not the CEO.

Large private corporations with at least $100 million in average annual gross receipts must calculate and report their pay ratio under Treasury rules, so the tax reaches private firms, not just public ones; smaller private companies are exempt.
The bill orders Treasury to write anti-avoidance rules, including to prevent companies from gaming the ratio by using contractors instead of employees.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with high CEO-to-worker pay gaps — and by extension their shareholders, who would see the higher tax reduce corporate earnings. Companies could avoid the tax by narrowing the gap, which is the intended effect, but companies that keep extreme pay ratios would owe more.
analysis.who_pays_short: Shareholders of large high pay-gap corporations

drawbacks.text: The surcharge is modest relative to the size of executive pay packages, so the biggest pay-gap firms could absorb the extra tax (a few tenths of a percent of revenue for even a 5-point rate increase on taxable income) rather than change pay structures, making the tax more of a revenue raiser than a pay-gap fixer.

Companies may respond by reshaping compensation in ways the tax does not measure — for example, shifting workers to contractor arrangements, which the bill tries to block by regulation but which enforcement would have to catch in practice.
Because the ratio is averaged over five years, recent changes in a company's pay structure take years to show up in its tax bill, slowing the incentive's effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks CEO-to-worker pay gaps through the tax code with a graduated surcharge and at least some built-in defenses against gaming. Its main honest weakness is that the penalty is small compared with the pay gaps it targets, so its practical power depends on whether companies would narrow gaps to avoid even a modest tax — a bet, not a guarantee. As a signal and a modest revenue measure it is straightforward; as a wage-boosting tool it is uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee in September 2025, and the committee has not scheduled any markup or hearing on it; since Congress is still in session, it could still move, but at this point it is sitting in committee with no action taken.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the bill on September 11, 2025, with 19 other original Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation.
No further action — no markup, hearing, or vote — has been recorded since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: At this stage, no outcome has occurred. The companies that would owe the surcharge — large corporations with extreme CEO-to-worker pay ratios — are better off for now, since the tax has not advanced and never became law.

for.name: Rep. Rashida Tlaib
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Rep. Chellie Pingree, Rep. Jared Huffman, and 28 other House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; no Republican cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 supporters are Democrats — sponsor plus 29 cosponsors — and no Republican has signed on, so the bill's support runs entirely along party lines so far.

industries.industry: Large corporations with high CEO-to-worker pay gaps (tech, finance, retail chains, fast food)
industries.note: These firms would owe a 0.5-to-5 percentage-point corporate tax surcharge for as long as their executive-to-median-worker pay ratio stays above 50-to-1. Their interest in avoiding that tax runs against workers whose pay would need to rise (or executives' pay fall) for the tax to disappear.

industries.industry: Public-company shareholders and large private companies near the $100 million revenue threshold
industries.note: Shareholders bear the tax through lower after-tax earnings; large private companies ($100M+ revenue) face new pay-ratio reporting and potential liability, while smaller private firms are exempt. Compliance costs are real but modest, and any company can escape the tax entirely by narrowing its pay gap.

analysis.trajectory: Bills to amend the tax code that are introduced by minority-party members with no cosponsors from the majority almost never reach a vote; Ways and Means' chair controls whether anything gets a markup. Unless pay-gap politics shifts or the bill picks up broad support, it will likely remain in committee through the end of the 119th Congress.
